Course guide

AE 101 - Foundations of Aeronautical Engineering
Practice template, not an approved institutional syllabus.

Learning outcomes
Define requirements and evidence; trace calculations and units; interpret force models; compare resources; communicate defensible recommendations.

Study route
Prelim: engineering practice and units.
Midterm: forces, motion and assumptions.
Semifinals: materials and resource decisions.
Finals: integrated verification and reporting.

Assessments
8 quizzes, 4 activities and 4 examinations open as selection forms in the app. Choose one answer per question, review and submit. Results show correct answers out of the total and a percentage. Completed forms collapse to a result; Review shows your selections.
One submission is recorded per form revision. Reading completion is separate from achievement. No aircraft operation or maintenance release is authorized by this classroom exercise.

Instructor setup
Add an assessment, write questions and choices, select the correct answers and publish. Set eligible student IDs and test the student view. Use approved classroom content for institutional teaching.
Suggested planning weights: quizzes 20%, activities 30%, examinations 50%, applied to category averages outside the app. Confirm institutional policy; the app does not calculate a weighted course grade.

resources.text:
AE 101 - Foundations of Aeronautical Engineering
Prelim | Weeks 1-4
Original classroom practice template; not an approved syllabus.

Prelim - Lesson 1: Engineering evidence

Outcome O1: distinguish a requirement, evidence and an assumption.
An engineering brief states what a solution must achieve, the limits it must respect and how success will be checked. A requirement is testable; an assumption is a condition taken as true until checked. A measurement is useful evidence only when its method, units and limits are known.
Classroom case: a model-aircraft storage rack must hold six models within a supplied floor-space limit. 'Looks strong' is not an acceptance criterion. 'Supports the stated classroom load without permanent deformation in the specified test' identifies a measurable outcome, but the instructor must define the load, setup and limits.
Record the document title, revision and source before using a table. Conflicting versions require clarification rather than silent mixing.
Practice: write one requirement, one assumption and one evidence item for the storage-rack brief. Identify what you would ask the instructor before calculating.

Prelim - Lesson 2: Units and records

Outcome O2: convert units and show a traceable calculation.
Write the quantity, symbol and unit before substituting numbers. A calculation should allow another student to follow the input data, conversion, equation and conclusion.
Worked example: 2.4 m = 2400 mm because 1 m = 1000 mm. Show the conversion factor so units cancel. Do not add a length in metres directly to a length recorded in millimetres.
Synthetic dataset: lengths 1200 mm, 0.8 m and 50 cm. Express each in metres before adding them. Report an appropriate number of digits rather than implying greater precision than the inputs provide.
A useful calculation record includes the data source or supplied dataset, assumptions, steps, units and one reasonableness check. Correct arithmetic with the wrong unit is still an incorrect result.
Practice: prepare a conversion table and explain how a unit error could change a classroom decision.

AE 101 - Foundations of Aeronautical Engineering
Midterm | Weeks 5-8
Original classroom practice template; not an approved syllabus.

Midterm - Lesson 3: Simple force models

Outcome O3: interpret a stated force model.
Use a free-body diagram to identify the forces acting on the object being studied. State the positive direction, magnitude and unit for each force. A force balance describes the model under its assumptions; it does not prove that a real aircraft is safe.
Worked classroom example: two horizontal forces of 12 N and 7 N act in opposite directions on a model cart. If right is positive and 12 N acts right, the net force is +5 N.
For an idealized aircraft in steady, level, unaccelerated flight, the simplified model balances lift with weight and thrust with drag. Changing the assumptions can change the balance.
Practice: sketch arrows for a cart pulled right by 18 N against a leftward 11 N resistance. Explain what the model leaves out and what further data would be needed to predict acceleration.

Midterm - Lesson 4: Motion and assumptions

Outcomes O2-O3: relate distance, time and average speed under stated conditions.
Average speed equals total distance divided by elapsed time. It is not automatically the speed at every instant. Define the interval and use consistent units.
Worked example: a model cart covers 24 m in 6 s. Its average speed is 4 m/s. This observation alone does not establish constant speed or acceleration.
Synthetic observations: trial A covers 30 m in 10 s; trial B covers 42 m in 12 s. Compare average speeds and list two measurement limitations, such as timing resolution and distance marking.
A model should be checked against evidence. If a measured result differs from a prediction, review assumptions, inputs, method and measurement uncertainty before changing a convenient number.
Practice: describe a repeatable classroom measurement method and explain why repeating a trial can reveal variability.

AE 101 - Foundations of Aeronautical Engineering
Semifinals | Weeks 9-12
Original classroom practice template; not an approved syllabus.

Semifinals - Lesson 5: Material comparisons

Outcome O4: compare alternatives using the same basis.
A comparison is meaningful when candidates meet the same stated function and constraints. Mass alone does not establish strength, durability, suitability or approval.
For a supplied volume, estimated mass equals density multiplied by volume. Keep units consistent.
Worked example: an imaginary classroom material with density 1200 kg/m3 occupying 0.002 m3 has estimated mass 2.4 kg. This arithmetic is not a qualification of the material.
Synthetic candidates for the same 0.001 m3 component: P has density 1600 kg/m3 and supplied cost PHP 180; Q has density 2400 kg/m3 and cost PHP 140. These fictional figures are task inputs, not market prices.
Practice: calculate both masses, compare the trade-off and identify missing strength/manufacturing data before recommending either candidate.

Semifinals - Lesson 6: Resource decisions

Outcomes O1/O4: justify a decision under explicit constraints.
Start with non-negotiable requirements, then compare eligible alternatives. A low cost does not compensate for failing a required limit. Show which evidence supports each judgment.
Synthetic procurement exercise: option A costs PHP 240 per unit and needs 2 hours assembly; option B costs PHP 200 per unit and needs 3 hours. Four units are needed. The classroom budget is PHP 1000 and assembly allowance is 10 hours. These figures are fictional.
Calculate total cost and time for each option. Identify which meets both limits, then state what remains unverified. A decision matrix can use columns for requirement, supplied evidence, pass/fail and uncertainty.
Practice: explain how your recommendation changes if the budget becomes PHP 850. If neither option meets all limits, request a revised brief rather than claiming success.

AE 101 - Foundations of Aeronautical Engineering
Finals | Weeks 13-16
Original classroom practice template; not an approved syllabus.

Finals - Lesson 7: Integration and validation

Outcomes O1-O5: connect a brief to a defensible test plan.
A useful engineering report links each requirement to evidence and a stated acceptance criterion. Separate predicted, measured and unverified results. A successful drawing or calculation does not establish field performance.
For a fictional classroom model carrier, plan checks for capacity, dimensions, estimated mass, cost and documentation quality. Define the setup, inputs, observation and pass/fail rule for each check. State who reviews unresolved assumptions.
Worked planning example: 'Compare the measured width with the supplied maximum using the stated measuring method; record the value and uncertainty.' The numerical limit must come from the brief, not an arbitrary change made after the result.
Practice: prepare a requirement-to-test table and explain what you would do when a required check is unavailable. Report it as unverified rather than passed.

Finals - Lesson 8: Technical communication

Outcome O5: communicate a recommendation with traceable limits.
Lead with the recommendation, then show the requirement, evidence and reasoning that support it. Include units, input sources, assumptions, uncertainty, unresolved checks and the next action. Use a concise table when comparing alternatives.
A report should let another person reproduce the analysis without guessing what a number means. Keep document revisions and distinguish original work from borrowed material.
When evidence is incomplete, make a conditional recommendation. Explain which additional result could change the decision; do not use confident language to conceal a missing check.
Practice: rewrite 'The carrier is perfect' as a bounded conclusion that identifies what was reviewed, what was measured and what remains unverified. Review a peer's fictional report for a missing unit, unsupported assumption and unclear acceptance criterion.
